newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: New Afghan rulers promise to pay laid-off women.
newsitem.headline: New Afghan rulers promise to pay laid-off women.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic movement, in a display of leniency, said on Monday all working women laid off for religious reasons would continue to be paid.

A decree issued by the Taleban's supreme leader Mullah Mohammad Omar from his headquarters in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar and quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said women told not to come to their offices would receive their salaries at home.
It was not immediately clear for how long such salaries would be paid.
The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) also quoted a Taleban spokesman as saying his movement had not denied women the right to education.
How could the Taleban, which in the Pashtu language means seekers or pupils and which grew out of Islamic theology schools, deny anybody the right to receive education, he was quoted as asking.
He said adult girls would definitely be given medical education as was being done now in the other main Taleban-held towns of Kandahar and Herat.
Other details about the role of women would be sorted out in the light of Fatwas, or decrees, from religious scholars, he said.
The Taleban captured Kabul on Friday and set up an interim ruling council vowing to turn Afghanistan into an Islamic state. It now controls about three-quarters of the country.
In orders issued after capturing the capital, the Taleban barred women from workplaces and told them not to leave their homes without wearing the Islamic "hejab" veil.

On Sunday it also ordered all men employed in government offices and the military to grow long beards and banned any Islamic funeral service for executed former president Najibullah because it said he was a communist.
Witnesses said at least four women had been beaten in public for violating Islamic dress codes by Taleban fighters wielding long chains in three separate incidents on Sunday.
Aid workers said one woman was beaten opposite the Jumhuriyet hospital in Kabul as her small son watched in tears.
Two other women were beaten near the Pul-i-Khishti mosque in central Kabul and a fourth in the Taye-maskan area, witnesses said.

The Taleban's fundamentalist decrees were announced by Kabul Radio hours after the special U.N. envoy to Afghanistan, Norbert Holl, said he saw hopeful signs in talks with the Islamist rulers on such issues as women's work outside the home.
